title: NEET PG — Pediatrics | Pediatric Oncology
description: Subject-wise test on Pediatric Oncology (Pediatrics) for NEET PG. 35Q.
subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 6-year-old child with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) on maintenance chemotherapy presents to the emergency department with a temperature of 38.5°C. His absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is 450 cells/µL. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Administer antipyretics and observe for 24 hours.
options.explanation: Delaying antibiotic therapy in febrile neutropenia can lead to rapid deterioration and sepsis.

options.text: Obtain blood cultures and start broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics immediately.
options.explanation: This is the standard of care for febrile neutropenia in pediatric oncology patients to prevent sepsis.

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture to rule out CNS infection.
options.explanation: Lumbar puncture is not the initial step in febrile neutropenia unless there are specific neurological signs or symptoms.

options.text: Discharge with oral antibiotics and advise follow-up.
options.explanation: Oral antibiotics are insufficient in neutropenic patients due to poor absorption and high risk of severe infection.

questions.explanation: In a febrile neutropenic child with ALL, the risk of overwhelming infection is high due to immunosuppression. Immediate administration of broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics is critical to cover potential gram-negative and gram-positive organisms, as per febrile neutropenia guidelines.
questions.hint: Consider the risk of severe infection in neutropenic patients and the need for urgent antibiotic coverage.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy undergoing chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia presents to the emergency department with a single oral temperature of 38.5°C. His absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is 400 cells/µL. He appears well and denies any specific symptoms. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Administer oral broad-spectrum antibiotics and discharge home with close follow-up.
options.explanation: Oral antibiotics are insufficient in febrile neutropenia due to poor absorption and the need for rapid, high-dose systemic coverage.

options.text: Admit for intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics after obtaining blood cultures.
options.explanation: This is the standard of care for febrile neutropenia in pediatric oncology patients to prevent sepsis and complications.

options.text: Start antipyretics and observe for 24 hours before deciding on antibiotics.
options.explanation: Delaying antibiotics in febrile neutropenia can lead to rapid deterioration and sepsis.

options.text: Perform a full septic workup including lumbar puncture before starting antibiotics.
options.explanation: While a full workup is important, antibiotics should not be delayed while awaiting procedures like lumbar puncture in febrile neutropenia.

questions.explanation: This child has chemotherapy-induced neutropenia (ANC < 500 cells/µL) with fever, which is a medical emergency. Febrile neutropenia requires immediate admission for intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics after obtaining blood cultures to prevent rapid progression to sepsis.
questions.hint: Neutropenia (ANC < 500) with fever is a medical emergency requiring urgent IV antibiotics.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy undergoing chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia presents to the emergency department with a temperature of 38.5°C and an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 450 cells/µL. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Administer antipyretics and observe for 24 hours.
options.explanation: Observation without antibiotics is inappropriate in neutropenic fever due to high risk of sepsis.

options.text: Obtain blood cultures and initiate empiric broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics.
options.explanation: Correct. Blood cultures should be obtained, and empiric broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics should be initiated immediately in neutropenic fever.

options.text: Perform a chest X-ray and administer oral antibiotics.
options.explanation: Chest X-ray and oral antibiotics are not sufficient initial steps in neutropenic fever.

options.text: Discharge home with instructions to return if symptoms worsen.
options.explanation: Discharge without treatment is contraindicated in neutropenic fever due to high risk of rapid deterioration.

questions.explanation: This child presents with neutropenic fever, defined as a single oral temperature of ≥38.3°C (or ≥38.0°C sustained for >1 hour) in a patient with an ANC <500 cells/µL (or expected to fall below this level within 48 hours). Neutropenic fever is an oncologic emergency requiring prompt evaluation and initiation of empiric broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics after obtaining blood cultures, due to the high risk of rapid progression to sepsis and septic shock. Delay in antibiotic administration significantly increases morbidity and mortality.
questions.hint: Neutropenic fever is an oncologic emergency requiring immediate action.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 5-year-old child with newly diagnosed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia presents with sudden onset of facial swelling, periorbital edema, dilated superficial veins on the chest, and dyspnea. On examination, the child has a plethoric face and a positive Pemberton's sign (facial plethora and respiratory distress on arm elevation). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Anaphylaxis typically presents with acute urticaria, angioedema, and airway compromise, not chronic venous congestion signs.
Angioedema involves localized swelling without the chronic venous congestion signs seen here.
Correct. The clinical presentation is classic for SVCS due to mediastinal mass compression of the superior vena cava.
Congestive heart failure would present with systemic and pulmonary edema but not the specific upper body venous congestion signs seen here.

questions.explanation: The constellation of facial swelling, periorbital edema, dilated chest veins, dyspnea, and a positive Pemberton's sign in a child with a mediastinal mass (common in T-cell ALL) is classic for Superior Vena Cava Syndrome (SVCS). This emergency results from compression or obstruction of the superior vena cava, impairing venous return from the head, neck, and upper extremities. Anaphylaxis and angioedema would have a more acute onset, typically with urticaria and airway compromise, but less likely the chronic venous congestion signs. Congestive heart failure would present with signs of systemic and pulmonary edema but less specific to the upper body and face in this manner.
questions.hint: Consider oncologic emergencies in children with mediastinal masses and upper body symptoms.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy with a large mediastinal mass diagnosed as T-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia is scheduled to start chemotherapy. Pre-treatment labs show a WBC count of 250,000/µL, LDH 3500 U/L, uric acid 12 mg/dL, potassium 5.8 mEq/L, and creatinine 1.5 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management strategy to prevent tumor lysis syndrome?

options.explanation: Allopurinol is insufficient for high-risk TLS with existing hyperuricemia; rasburicase is preferred.
Correct. Aggressive IV hydration and rasburicase are the most appropriate initial steps for high-risk TLS.
Oral hydration is insufficient, and allopurinol is not preferred for high-risk TLS with existing hyperuricemia.
Dialysis is not the initial step; it is reserved for severe, refractory electrolyte imbalances or renal failure.

questions.explanation: This patient has high-risk features for tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) due to a very high tumor burden (large mediastinal mass, WBC 250,000/µL) and already has evidence of electrolyte derangements (hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, elevated creatinine suggesting early renal injury) consistent with established or impending TLS. Aggressive intravenous hydration is crucial for all patients at risk or with TLS. Rasburicase is preferred over allopurinol in high-risk patients or those with established hyperuricemia because it rapidly breaks down existing uric acid, whereas allopurinol only prevents new uric acid formation. Dialysis is reserved for severe, refractory electrolyte imbalances, particularly hyperkalemia or renal failure, and is not the initial step.
questions.hint: High-risk TLS requires aggressive hydration and uric acid management with rasburicase.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 6-year-old girl with a known diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma of the spine presents with new-onset severe back pain, progressive weakness in both legs, and difficulty urinating. On examination, she has decreased sensation below the T10 dermatome and diminished deep tendon reflexes in her lower limbs. What is the most immediate therapeutic intervention indicated?

options.explanation: While an urgent MRI is essential, it is not the most immediate therapeutic intervention.
Correct. High-dose IV corticosteroids are the most immediate therapeutic intervention to reduce spinal cord edema.
Surgical decompression is important but not the immediate first step; corticosteroids should be given first.
Antibiotics are not indicated unless there is suspicion of infection.

questions.explanation: This child presents with signs and symptoms of acute spinal cord compression, an oncologic emergency. While an urgent MRI of the spine is essential for definitive diagnosis and localization, the most immediate therapeutic intervention to prevent irreversible neurological damage is high-dose intravenous corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone). Corticosteroids reduce peritumoral edema, thereby alleviating pressure on the spinal cord. Emergency surgical decompression or radiation therapy would be considered after imaging and in conjunction with steroid administration, but steroids provide the fastest initial symptomatic relief. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are not indicated unless there is suspicion of infection.
questions.hint: Spinal cord compression is an oncologic emergency requiring immediate corticosteroids.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is NOT typically associated with tumor lysis syndrome (TLS)?

options.explanation: Hyperkalemia is a classic feature of TLS due to release of intracellular potassium.
Hyperphosphatemia is a classic feature of TLS due to release of intracellular phosphate.
Correct. Hypercalcemia is not typically associated with TLS; hypocalcemia is more common due to phosphate binding calcium.
Hyperuricemia is a classic feature of TLS due to breakdown of nucleic acids.

questions.explanation: Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is characterized by the rapid breakdown of malignant cells, leading to the release of intracellular components into the bloodstream. This typically results in a constellation of metabolic abnormalities including hyperkalemia (release of intracellular potassium), hyperphosphatemia (release of intracellular phosphate), hypocalcemia (due to phosphate binding calcium), and hyperuricemia (breakdown of nucleic acids). Hypercalcemia is generally associated with other paraneoplastic syndromes or bone metastases, not TLS itself.
questions.hint: TLS typically causes hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and hyperuricemia.

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy with Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) presents to the emergency department with a WBC count of 400,000/µL, severe lethargy, headache, and blurred vision. His platelet count is 20,000/µL, and there are no signs of active bleeding. What is the most appropriate initial management for his hyperleukocytosis?

options.explanation: Platelet transfusion is not indicated unless there is active bleeding or prior to an invasive procedure, as it can worsen hyperviscosity.
Leukapheresis is important but not the initial step; chemotherapy and hydration should be prioritized.
Antibiotics are not the primary treatment for leukostasis; they are for fever/infection.

options.text: Intravenous hydration and immediate initiation of chemotherapy
options.explanation: Correct. Aggressive IV hydration and immediate chemotherapy are the most appropriate initial steps for symptomatic hyperleukocytosis.

questions.explanation: This patient presents with hyperleukocytosis and symptoms suggestive of leukostasis (severe lethargy, headache, blurred vision), which is a medical emergency. While leukapheresis can rapidly reduce the WBC count, it is often reserved for severe symptomatic leukostasis, particularly in AML where the blasts are larger and more prone to sludging. The most appropriate initial management for symptomatic hyperleukocytosis, especially in AML, involves aggressive intravenous hydration to prevent tumor lysis syndrome and reduce blood viscosity, combined with immediate initiation of specific induction chemotherapy. Chemotherapy is the definitive treatment to reduce the blast count. Platelet transfusion is not indicated unless there is active bleeding or prior to an invasive procedure, as it can worsen hyperviscosity. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are for fever/infection, not the primary treatment for leukostasis.
questions.hint: Hyperleukocytosis with leukostasis requires immediate chemotherapy and hydration; leukapheresis is secondary.

questions.question: A 9-year-old girl undergoing intensive chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia develops fever, severe right lower quadrant abdominal pain, and bloody diarrhea. On examination, her abdomen is distended and tender, particularly in the right iliac fossa. Her absolute neutrophil count is 50 cells/µL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Acute appendicitis is less likely given the profound neutropenia and bloody diarrhea.
Clostridium difficile colitis is possible but less likely to cause such severe localized pain and necrosis.
Correct. The clinical presentation is classic for typhlitis in a neutropenic patient.
Intussusception is less common in this age group and clinical context.

questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of fever, severe right lower quadrant abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and profound neutropenia in a child undergoing chemotherapy is highly suggestive of typhlitis, also known as neutropenic enterocolitis. This condition involves inflammation and necrosis of the cecum and ascending colon. While acute appendicitis can present similarly, the profound neutropenia and bloody diarrhea point more towards typhlitis. Clostridium difficile colitis is possible but less likely to cause such severe localized pain and often lacks the necrotic component. Intussusception is less common in this age group and clinical context and would typically present with intermittent colicky pain and 'currant jelly' stools.
questions.hint: Typhlitis is a common complication in neutropenic patients with abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy with high-risk neuroblastoma presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of increasing irritability, vomiting, and a new onset of head tilt. On examination, he is lethargic, has papilledema, and an altered Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score. His blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg, and heart rate is 60 bpm. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate medical management?

options.text: Administer a bolus of intravenous fluids.
options.explanation: IV fluids may worsen cerebral edema and are not the immediate treatment for increased ICP.
Antibiotics are not indicated unless there is suspicion of infection.

options.text: Administer intravenous mannitol or hypertonic saline.
options.explanation: Correct. Osmotic agents like mannitol or hypertonic saline are the most appropriate immediate management for increased ICP.
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in the presence of increased ICP due to risk of brain herniation.

questions.explanation: This child presents with clear signs of increased intracranial pressure (ICP) including irritability, vomiting, lethargy, papilledema, altered GCS, and Cushing's triad (hypertension and bradycardia). Given his history of neuroblastoma, brain metastases or direct tumor extension are likely causes. The most immediate medical management for acute ICP elevation is to reduce brain edema using osmotic agents like intravenous mannitol or hypertonic saline. A bolus of intravenous fluids may worsen cerebral edema. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are not indicated unless there is suspicion of infection. Emergency lumbar puncture is contraindicated in the presence of increased ICP due to risk of brain herniation.
questions.hint: Increased intracranial pressure requires immediate osmotic therapy to reduce brain edema.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with fever, pallor, and multiple bruises over the extremities. On examination, he has hepatosplenomegaly and petechiae. Complete blood count reveals Hb 8.2 g/dL, TLC 15,000/cmm (blasts 30%), and platelets 20,000/cmm. Peripheral smear shows 30% blasts with Auer rods. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: ALL typically has lymphoblasts without Auer rods.
Auer rods in blasts are diagnostic of AML.
ITP presents with isolated thrombocytopenia without blasts.
Aplastic anemia shows pancytopenia without blasts.

questions.explanation: Presence of Auer rods in blasts is diagnostic of AML. ALL typically has lymphoblasts without Auer rods. ITP presents with isolated thrombocytopenia without blasts. Aplastic anemia shows pancytopenia without blasts.
questions.hint: Auer rods are pathognomonic for myeloid lineage.

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl presents with sudden onset of right-sided abdominal pain and vomiting. Ultrasound abdomen reveals a heterogeneous mass in the right kidney. Urine examination shows hematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Neuroblastoma is usually suprarenal and crosses midline.
Wilm’s tumor presents with painless abdominal mass, hematuria, and hypertension.
Renal cell carcinoma is rare in this age group.
Mesoblastic nephroma is benign and presents in infants.

questions.explanation: Wilm’s tumor presents with painless abdominal mass, hematuria, and hypertension. Neuroblastoma is usually suprarenal and crosses midline. Renal cell carcinoma is rare in this age group. Mesoblastic nephroma is benign and presents in infants.
questions.hint: Consider common pediatric renal tumors.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy with a history of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) on maintenance therapy presents with fever and neutropenia (ANC 300/cmm). The child is hemodynamically stable. What is the next best step in management?

options.explanation: Oral antibiotics are insufficient for neutropenic fever.

options.text: Admit and start empirical IV antibiotics (cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam)
options.explanation: Neutropenic fever requires admission and empirical IV antibiotics covering Pseudomonas.
Empirical antifungals are reserved for persistent fever after 4-7 days.
Bone marrow is not indicated at this stage.

questions.explanation: Neutropenic fever in a child with cancer is an oncologic emergency requiring admission and empirical IV antibiotics covering Pseudomonas. Oral antibiotics are insufficient. Empirical antifungals are reserved for persistent fever after 4-7 days. Bone marrow is not indicated at this stage.
questions.hint: Neutropenic fever requires urgent IV antibiotics.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 3-year-old child presents with a mediastinal mass causing superior vena cava syndrome. Biopsy reveals small round blue cells with CD99 positivity. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: NHL has different immunophenotypes.
Hodgkin lymphoma has different immunophenotypes.
CD99 positivity and mediastinal mass are characteristic of Ewing sarcoma/PNET.
Neuroblastoma typically arises from adrenal gland or paravertebral region.

questions.explanation: CD99 positivity and mediastinal mass are characteristic of Ewing sarcoma/PNET. NHL and Hodgkin lymphoma have different immunophenotypes. Neuroblastoma typically arises from adrenal gland or paravertebral region.
questions.hint: CD99 positivity is key for diagnosis.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy develops severe headache and vomiting after receiving intrathecal methotrexate for ALL. On examination, he has nuchal rigidity and altered sensorium. CSF analysis shows WBC 100/cmm (lymphocytes), protein 60 mg/dL, and glucose 60 mg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Bacterial meningitis has low glucose and high neutrophils.
Intrathecal methotrexate can cause chemical (aseptic) meningitis.
Fungal meningitis is rare in this setting.
Leukemic meningitis would show blasts in CSF.

questions.explanation: Intrathecal methotrexate can cause chemical (aseptic) meningitis. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose. Bacterial meningitis has low glucose and high neutrophils. Fungal meningitis is rare in this setting. Leukemic meningitis would show blasts in CSF.
questions.hint: Consider drug-induced complications in oncology patients.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl presents with a 3-month history of progressive pallor, fatigue, and bruising. Examination reveals generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Bone marrow aspiration shows >20% blasts with CD10 and CD19 positivity. What is the most likely immunophenotype of these blasts?

options.explanation: T-ALL would have T-cell markers (CD2, CD3, CD7).
Myeloid markers (MPO, CD13, CD33) are seen in AML.
CD19 and CD10 positivity with TdT is characteristic of B-cell ALL.
T-ALL would have T-cell markers (CD2, CD3, CD7).

questions.explanation: CD19 and CD10 positivity with TdT is characteristic of B-cell ALL. T-ALL would have T-cell markers (CD2, CD3, CD7). Myeloid markers (MPO, CD13, CD33) are seen in AML. CD34 and TdT are seen in both but not specific.
questions.hint: CD19 and CD10 are B-cell markers.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 2-year-old child presents with sudden onset of right leg pain and inability to bear weight. X-ray shows a lytic lesion in the distal femur with a periosteal reaction. MRI reveals a soft tissue mass. What is the next best step in diagnosis?

options.explanation: Biopsy is done after imaging.
Next step is to look for metastases with bone scan and chest X-ray.
PET-CT is not first-line.
ALP may be elevated in osteosarcoma but is not diagnostic.

questions.explanation: Lytic lesion with periosteal reaction and soft tissue mass suggests a malignant bone tumor (osteosarcoma or Ewing sarcoma). Next step is to look for metastases with bone scan and chest X-ray. Biopsy is done after imaging. PET-CT is not first-line. ALP may be elevated in osteosarcoma but is not diagnostic.
questions.hint: Metastatic workup is essential for bone tumors.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 6-month-old infant presents with failure to thrive, recurrent infections, and a large mediastinal mass. CBC shows anemia, thrombocytopenia, and lymphocytosis. Flow cytometry reveals CD45 dim, CD19+, CD20+, and TdT+ cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: T-ALL would lack CD19/CD20.
CD19 and CD20 positivity with TdT indicates B-cell ALL.
CML has different immunophenotypes and clinical presentations.
JMML has different immunophenotypes and clinical presentations.

questions.explanation: CD19 and CD20 positivity with TdT indicates B-cell ALL. T-ALL would lack CD19/CD20. CML and JMML have different immunophenotypes and clinical presentations.
questions.hint: CD19 and CD20 are B-cell markers.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy with a history of Hodgkin lymphoma presents with fever, cough, and dyspnea 4 weeks after completing chemotherapy. Chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.explanation: Immunocompromised status after chemotherapy predisposes to PCP.
Bacterial pneumonia is less likely without neutropenia.
Fungal pneumonia is less likely without neutropenia.
Radiation pneumonitis occurs during or shortly after radiation therapy, not weeks later.

questions.explanation: Immunocompromised status after chemotherapy predisposes to PCP. Bacterial and fungal pneumonias are less likely without neutropenia. Radiation pneumonitis occurs during or shortly after radiation therapy, not weeks later.
questions.hint: Consider opportunistic infections in immunocompromised patients.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 3-year-old child presents with a painless neck mass for 2 months. Fine needle aspiration cytology shows small round blue cells with high N:C ratio. Immunohistochemistry is positive for synaptophysin and chromogranin. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: NHL would show lymphoid markers.
Rhabdomyosarcoma shows muscle markers.
Synaptophysin and chromogranin positivity indicates neuroendocrine origin, typical of neuroblastoma.
Germ cell tumors have different markers (e.g., AFP, beta-hCG).

questions.explanation: Synaptophysin and chromogranin positivity indicates neuroendocrine origin, typical of neuroblastoma. NHL would show lymphoid markers. Rhabdomyosarcoma shows muscle markers. Germ cell tumors have different markers (e.g., AFP, beta-hCG).
questions.hint: Synaptophysin and chromogranin are neuroendocrine markers.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy with newly diagnosed T-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia presents with lethargy, vomiting, and oliguria. His initial labs show: K+ 6.8 mEq/L, PO4 7.2 mg/dL, Ca 6.5 mg/dL, Uric Acid 12 mg/dL, Creatinine 2.5 mg/dL. He has just received his first dose of chemotherapy. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate immediate step in his management?

options.text: Oral allopurinol and intravenous fluids at maintenance rate
options.explanation: Allopurinol is not sufficient for acute TLS management as it does not break down existing uric acid. Maintenance fluids are inadequate for this high-risk patient.

options.text: Intravenous fluids at 2-3 times maintenance rate and rasburicase
options.explanation: Aggressive hydration and rasburicase are the cornerstones of TLS management to rapidly lower uric acid and prevent complications like renal failure and arrhythmias.

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate for hypocalcemia and oral phosphate binders
options.explanation: Calcium correction is not the priority in acute TLS, and phosphate binders are not the immediate step. Calcium correction may worsen complications if given in the presence of hyperphosphatemia.

options.text: Hemodialysis to correct electrolyte imbalances immediately
options.explanation: Hemodialysis is reserved for severe or refractory cases of TLS but is not the first-line immediate step. Aggressive hydration and rasburicase should be attempted first.

questions.explanation: The patient is at high risk for Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS) due to high uric acid, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia. Immediate management includes aggressive hydration (2-3 times maintenance) with IV fluids to promote diuresis, and administration of rasburicase (a recombinant urate oxidase) to rapidly lower uric acid levels. Allopurinol is not sufficient for acute TLS management as it does not break down existing uric acid. Calcium correction is not the priority in this setting.
questions.hint: Consider the immediate risk of Tumor Lysis Syndrome in this patient with high uric acid and electrolyte imbalances.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy, undergoing chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia, presents with a fever of 38.5°C and absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 400 cells/µL. He is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Oral broad-spectrum antibiotics and close outpatient monitoring.
options.explanation: Oral antibiotics are insufficient in febrile neutropenia due to poor absorption and high risk of severe infection.

options.text: Intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and hospital admission.
options.explanation: This is the standard of care for febrile neutropenia in pediatric oncology patients to prevent sepsis and other complications.
Delaying antibiotics in febrile neutropenia can lead to rapid deterioration and sepsis.

options.text: Blood culture and discharge with instructions to return if symptoms worsen.
options.explanation: Discharging a febrile neutropenic patient without immediate antibiotics is unsafe due to the high risk of infection.

questions.explanation: Febrile neutropenia in a pediatric oncology patient requires immediate intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and hospital admission due to the high risk of severe infection.
questions.hint: Consider the definition of febrile neutropenia and its management in immunocompromised patients.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy with newly diagnosed T-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia presents with facial plethora, neck vein distension, and hoarseness. His chest X-ray shows a large anterior mediastinal mass. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management step for this patient?

options.explanation: Chemotherapy initiation is not the immediate priority as it may not rapidly relieve airway obstruction and could worsen symptoms in the short term.
Steroids may be used later in the treatment but are not the immediate priority for airway management.

options.text: Urgent radiation therapy to the mediastinum
options.explanation: Radiation therapy is not typically the first-line immediate intervention for airway compromise in this setting.

options.text: Secure airway and provide supportive care
options.explanation: The immediate priority is to secure the airway and provide supportive care to prevent respiratory arrest due to compression by the mediastinal mass.

questions.explanation: This patient presents with signs and symptoms of Superior Vena Cava Syndrome (SVCS) due to compression of the mediastinal mass on the superior vena cava and trachea. Immediate priority is to secure the airway and provide supportive care to prevent respiratory compromise before initiating definitive treatment.
questions.hint: Consider the risk of airway obstruction in mediastinal masses.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy, recently diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and about to start chemotherapy, presents with lethargy, poor feeding, and nausea. Laboratory investigations reveal: Uric acid: 12 mg/dL, Potassium: 6.2 mEq/L, Phosphate: 7.0 mg/dL, Calcium: 6.8 mg/dL, Creatinine: 1.8 mg/dL. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate initial management step for this patient?

options.explanation: Calcium gluconate is indicated for symptomatic hypocalcemia or severe hyperkalemia-induced cardiac changes, but not as the first step for this overall picture.

options.text: Initiate aggressive intravenous hydration with normal saline and allopurinol.
options.explanation: Aggressive intravenous hydration and allopurinol are the cornerstone of initial management for TLS.

options.text: Prepare for urgent hemodialysis due to renal failure.
options.explanation: Hemodialysis is reserved for refractory TLS, severe electrolyte imbalances unresponsive to medical management, or severe renal failure.

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct acidosis.
options.explanation: Sodium bicarbonate is generally avoided as it can precipitate calcium phosphate crystals in the renal tubules.

questions.explanation: This patient presents with classic laboratory findings of tumor lysis syndrome (TLS): hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia, along with acute kidney injury. The cornerstone of initial management for TLS is aggressive intravenous hydration (to increase urine output and promote excretion of metabolites) and allopurinol (to inhibit uric acid formation).
questions.hint: Tumor lysis syndrome is an oncologic emergency requiring immediate stabilization.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy with Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) on maintenance chemotherapy develops a fever of 38.5°C. His absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is 150/µL. He appears irritable but is hemodynamically stable. What is the *most urgent* initial management step?

options.text: Administer antipyretics and monitor vital signs closely.
options.explanation: Antipyretics alone do not address the underlying risk of overwhelming infection in neutropenia. Monitoring is insufficient without antibiotics.

options.text: Obtain blood cultures from at least two sites and administer empiric broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics.
options.explanation: This is the standard of care for febrile neutropenia: cultures to identify pathogens followed by immediate empiric antibiotics (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem) to cover gram-negative bacteria, which are the most common cause of sepsis in this setting.

options.text: Perform a chest X-ray and urinalysis to identify the source of infection.
options.explanation: While source identification is important, it should not delay the initiation of empiric antibiotics in a neutropenic child with fever. Imaging and urinalysis can be performed after antibiotics are started.

options.text: Administer granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) to boost neutrophil count.
options.explanation: G-CSF is not part of the immediate management of febrile neutropenia. Its role is limited to specific cases (e.g., prolonged neutropenia after chemotherapy) and does not replace the need for antibiotics.

questions.explanation: In a febrile neutropenic child with ANC <500/µL, the most urgent step is to initiate empiric broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour of presentation to prevent sepsis. Antipyretics alone are insufficient, and delaying antibiotics increases mortality risk. Source identification (e.g., cultures) should follow, not precede, antibiotic administration.
questions.hint: Neutropenic fever in oncology patients requires immediate empiric antibiotics regardless of hemodynamic stability.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy presents with fever, pallor, and easy bruising for 2 weeks. On examination, he has hepatosplenomegaly and petechiae. His complete blood count shows Hb 7.2 g/dL, WBC count 45,000/μL with 80% blasts, and platelet count 20,000/μL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Correct. Pancytopenia with blasts and organomegaly is characteristic of ALL.
Incorrect. ITP presents with isolated thrombocytopenia without blasts or organomegaly.
Incorrect. Aplastic anemia presents with pancytopenia but no blasts in the peripheral smear.
Incorrect. HUS presents with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and renal failure, not blasts or organomegaly.

questions.explanation: The clinical presentation with pancytopenia, blast cells, and organomegaly is classic for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). ITP presents with isolated thrombocytopenia, aplastic anemia with pancytopenia but no blasts, and HUS with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and renal failure.
questions.hint: Consider the presence of blasts in the peripheral smear and organomegaly.

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department with sudden onset of right-sided weakness and slurred speech. Her mother reports a history of recurrent infections but no significant trauma. MRI brain shows a large infarct in the left middle cerebral artery territory. Which of the following oncological conditions is most likely associated with this presentation?

options.explanation: Incorrect. AML is less commonly associated with stroke compared to ALL.
Incorrect. Neuroblastoma does not typically present with stroke.
Correct. ALL is associated with hyperleukocytosis and increased risk of stroke.
Incorrect. Wilms tumor does not typically present with stroke.

questions.explanation: Children with ALL are at risk of stroke due to hyperleukocytosis, leukostasis, and increased risk of thrombosis. Neuroblastoma and Wilms tumor do not typically present with stroke, and AML is less commonly associated compared to ALL.
questions.hint: Consider the association of stroke with hyperleukocytosis in pediatric leukemias.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy with a history of acute lymphoblastic leukemia is undergoing maintenance chemotherapy. He presents with fever of 38.5°C and neutropenia (ANC 200/μL). Blood cultures are pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.explanation: Incorrect. Oral antibiotics are insufficient in febrile neutropenia.

options.text: Administer broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour
options.explanation: Correct. Empiric IV antibiotics should be started within 1 hour in febrile neutropenia.

options.text: Wait for culture results before starting antibiotics
options.explanation: Incorrect. Cultures should not delay the initiation of antibiotics in febrile neutropenia.
Incorrect. G-CSF is not routinely indicated for initial management of febrile neutropenia.

questions.explanation: Febrile neutropenia in a pediatric oncology patient is a medical emergency. Empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem) should be started within 1 hour of presentation to prevent sepsis. Oral antibiotics are insufficient, cultures must not delay treatment, and G-CSF is not routinely indicated for initial management.
questions.hint: Consider the urgency of starting antibiotics in febrile neutropenia.

questions.question: A 10-year-old child presents with a 3-week history of progressive headache, vomiting, and ataxia. On examination, he has papilledema and truncal ataxia. MRI brain shows a posterior fossa mass with obstructive hydrocephalus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Correct. Medulloblastoma is the most common posterior fossa tumor in children.
Incorrect. Craniopharyngioma is typically suprasellar and does not present with posterior fossa symptoms.
Incorrect. Ependymoma arises from the ependymal lining of the ventricles and may not present with posterior fossa symptoms.
Incorrect. Pilocytic astrocytoma is usually hemispheric or suprasellar and less likely to cause obstructive hydrocephalus.

questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children, typically arising in the posterior fossa. It presents with obstructive hydrocephalus, headache, vomiting, and ataxia. Craniopharyngioma and pilocytic astrocytoma are usually suprasellar or hemispheric, and ependymoma often arises from the ependymal lining of the ventricles.
questions.hint: Consider the location and common pediatric brain tumors in the posterior fossa.

questions.question: A 3-month-old infant presents with a history of poor feeding, irritability, and rapid breathing. On examination, the heart rate is 220/min, respiratory rate is 60/min, and there is hepatomegaly. ECG shows narrow complex tachycardia with a ventricular rate of 220/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.explanation: Correct. Adenosine is the first-line treatment for acute SVT in infants.
Incorrect. Digoxin is not first-line for acute SVT.
Incorrect. Propranolol is not first-line for acute SVT.
Incorrect. Amiodarone is reserved for refractory cases.

questions.explanation: The infant has supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), the most common arrhythmia in children. Adenosine is the first-line treatment for acute SVT due to its rapid onset and short half-life. Digoxin and propranolol are not first-line in acute settings, and amiodarone is reserved for refractory cases.
questions.hint: Consider the first-line treatment for acute SVT in infants.

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl with a history of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) in remission presents with sudden onset of severe abdominal pain and distension. Ultrasound reveals free fluid in the abdomen. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this presentation?

options.explanation: Incorrect. Appendicitis is unlikely in a neutropenic patient with diffuse symptoms.
Incorrect. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is less common in this context.
Incorrect. Tumor lysis syndrome presents with metabolic abnormalities, not localized pain.
Correct. Typhlitis is a common complication in neutropenic leukemia patients.

questions.explanation: Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) is a common complication in children with leukemia during periods of profound neutropenia. It presents with abdominal pain, distension, and fever. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is less common, and tumor lysis syndrome typically presents with metabolic abnormalities rather than localized pain. Appendicitis is unlikely in a neutropenic patient with diffuse symptoms.
questions.hint: Consider complications of leukemia in neutropenic patients.

questions.question: A 2-year-old boy presents with a history of recurrent epistaxis and easy bruising over the past month. On examination, he has multiple ecchymoses and petechiae. His platelet count is 15,000/μL, and peripheral smear shows large platelets. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Incorrect. ALL presents with blast cells, not isolated thrombocytopenia.
Correct. ITP is the most common cause of isolated thrombocytopenia in children.
Incorrect. Aplastic anemia presents with pancytopenia, not isolated thrombocytopenia.
Incorrect. von Willebrand disease presents with mucocutaneous bleeding but normal platelet count.

questions.explanation: ITP is the most common cause of isolated thrombocytopenia in children, often following a viral illness. The presence of large platelets on smear supports the diagnosis. ALL presents with blast cells, aplastic anemia with pancytopenia, and von Willebrand disease with mucocutaneous bleeding but normal platelet count.
questions.hint: Consider the most common cause of isolated thrombocytopenia in children.

questions.question: A 6-year-old child with a history of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) develops sudden onset of chest pain, dyspnea, and hypoxia 2 days after starting induction chemotherapy. Chest X-ray shows bilateral diffuse infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.explanation: Incorrect. Pneumonia would typically have a more localized infiltrate.
Incorrect. Tumor lysis syndrome presents with metabolic abnormalities, not localized lung infiltrates.
Correct. Cytarabine can cause non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema or pneumonitis.
Incorrect. Pulmonary embolism is less common in this age group with these symptoms.

questions.explanation: Cytarabine, a common drug in ALL induction therapy, can cause non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema or pneumonitis. The timing (within days of starting chemotherapy) and diffuse bilateral infiltrates support this diagnosis. Pneumonia would typically have a more localized infiltrate, tumor lysis syndrome presents with metabolic abnormalities, and pulmonary embolism is less common in this age group.
questions.hint: Consider chemotherapy-induced complications in the lungs.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy presents with a 1-week history of fever, bone pain, and pallor. On examination, he has multiple tender bony swellings. His hemoglobin is 6.5 g/dL, WBC count is 25,000/μL with 30% blasts, and platelet count is 40,000/μL. Bone marrow biopsy shows 85% blasts. Which of the following immunophenotypes is most likely associated with this clinical picture?

options.explanation: Correct. B-ALL typically expresses CD19, CD10, and TdT.
Incorrect. These markers are associated with T-ALL, not B-ALL.
Incorrect. These markers suggest AML, not ALL.
Incorrect. CD20 is less specific than CD19 in ALL.

questions.explanation: The clinical picture is consistent with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), which typically expresses CD19, CD10, and TdT. T-ALL would express T-cell markers (CD3, CD7), and myeloid markers (CD13, CD33) suggest AML. CD20 is a B-cell marker but is less specific than CD19 in ALL.
questions.hint: Consider the immunophenotype of B-cell ALL.

questions.question: A 3-year-old girl presents with a history of fever, cough, and progressive respiratory distress over 48 hours. On examination, she has tachypnea, subcostal retractions, and decreased breath sounds on the right. Chest X-ray shows a large right-sided pleural effusion. Which of the following oncological emergencies is most likely responsible for this presentation?

options.explanation: Incorrect. SVC syndrome presents with facial swelling and distended neck veins.
Incorrect. Chemotherapy-induced pneumonitis would show diffuse infiltrates.

options.text: Malignant pleural effusion secondary to leukemia
options.explanation: Correct. Leukemia can cause malignant pleural effusions due to leukemic infiltration.
Incorrect. Pulmonary embolism is less likely in this age group with these symptoms.

questions.explanation: Children with leukemia can develop malignant pleural effusions due to leukemic infiltration or secondary to complications like infection (e.g., empyema) in neutropenic patients. Superior vena cava syndrome presents with facial swelling and distended neck veins, chemotherapy-induced pneumonitis would have diffuse infiltrates, and pulmonary embolism is less likely in this age group with these symptoms.
questions.hint: Consider complications of leukemia that can cause pleural effusion.

questions.question: A 5-year-old child undergoing chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia presents with a single oral temperature reading of 38.5°C. Her absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is 0.4 x 10^9/L. Which of the following best defines neutropenic fever in this patient?

options.text: Oral temperature ≥ 38.0°C sustained for 1 hour, with ANC < 0.5 x 10^9/L.
options.explanation: This option misses the single reading temperature threshold of ≥38.3°C.

options.text: Oral temperature ≥ 38.3°C (single reading) or ≥ 38.0°C sustained for 1 hour, with ANC < 0.5 x 10^9/L or expected to fall below 0.5 x 10^9/L within 48 hours.
options.explanation: This matches the standard definition of neutropenic fever as per IDSA guidelines.

options.text: Oral temperature ≥ 38.3°C (single reading), with ANC < 1.0 x 10^9/L.
options.explanation: This option incorrectly uses ANC < 1.0 x 10^9/L instead of < 0.5 x 10^9/L.

options.text: Oral temperature ≥ 38.0°C sustained for 1 hour, with ANC < 1.0 x 10^9/L.
options.explanation: This option incorrectly uses ANC < 1.0 x 10^9/L and misses the single reading temperature threshold of ≥38.3°C.

questions.explanation: This is the standard definition of neutropenic fever (also known as febrile neutropenia) as per infectious disease guidelines (e.g., IDSA), which is crucial for prompt recognition and management in oncology patients. The key components are a significant temperature elevation (single ≥38.3°C or sustained ≥38.0°C) and significant neutropenia (ANC <0.5 x 10^9/L or anticipated to be so).
questions.hint: Consider the temperature threshold and ANC criteria for neutropenic fever as per IDSA guidelines.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy with newly diagnosed T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia presents with facial swelling, distended neck veins, and respiratory distress. A chest X-ray shows a large anterior mediastinal mass. What is the MOST appropriate initial management step?

options.explanation: While intubation may be necessary, it is not the initial step. High-dose corticosteroids should be administered first to reduce tumor size and relieve airway compression.
Antibiotics are not the primary treatment for SVCS caused by a mediastinal mass. Corticosteroids are the first-line therapy.
High-dose corticosteroids are the most appropriate initial management to reduce tumor size and relieve airway compression in SVCS.

options.text: Obtain an urgent mediastinal biopsy for definitive diagnosis.
options.explanation: A biopsy is not the initial step in a patient with respiratory distress due to SVCS. Stabilization with corticosteroids is prioritized.

questions.explanation: In a patient with suspected Superior Vena Cava Syndrome (SVCS) due to a mediastinal mass, high-dose corticosteroids are the most appropriate initial management to reduce tumor size and relieve airway compression.
questions.hint: Consider the immediate risk of airway compromise in SVCS and the role of corticosteroids in reducing tumor size.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy with Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) on chemotherapy presents to the emergency department with a temperature of 38.8°C, chills, and malaise. His absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is 0.3 x 10^9/L. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate initial step in management?

options.text: Administer antipyretics and observe for 6 hours.
options.explanation: Antipyretics alone are insufficient; immediate antibiotics are required to prevent sepsis.

options.text: Obtain blood cultures and initiate broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics immediately.
options.explanation: Correct. Blood cultures and immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics are the standard of care for neutropenic fever.

options.text: Perform a chest X-ray and lumbar puncture before starting any treatment.
options.explanation: Diagnostic procedures should not delay antibiotic administration in neutropenic fever.

options.text: Send home with oral antibiotics and instruct to return if symptoms worsen.
options.explanation: Oral antibiotics are inadequate; inpatient IV antibiotics are required for neutropenic fever.

questions.explanation: This patient presents with neutropenic fever, defined as a single oral temperature of ≥38.3°C or a temperature of ≥38.0°C sustained for >1 hour in a patient with an ANC <0.5 x 10^9/L (or expected to fall to this level). It is a life-threatening emergency in oncology patients. The most appropriate initial step is to obtain blood cultures (from at least two sites, including central lines if present) and immediately initiate broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, even before culture results are available, due to the high risk of rapid progression to sepsis and septic shock. Delaying antibiotics increases mortality.
questions.hint: Neutropenic fever in oncology patients requires urgent antibiotic administration.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy with Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) on maintenance chemotherapy presents to the emergency department with a fever of 39.5°C. His absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is 300 cells/µL. He appears well, with no localizing signs of infection. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Administer oral broad-spectrum antibiotics and discharge home with close follow-up.
options.explanation: Oral antibiotics are not the immediate step for febrile neutropenia in oncology patients; IV antibiotics are required.

options.text: Obtain blood cultures and administer intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately.
options.explanation: This is the correct immediate management for febrile neutropenia in oncology patients.

options.text: Administer antipyretics and observe for 6-8 hours before deciding on antibiotics.
options.explanation: Observation without antibiotics is dangerous in febrile neutropenia due to high risk of rapid progression to sepsis.

options.text: Perform a full septic work-up including lumbar puncture, and then start antibiotics.
options.explanation: A full septic work-up including lumbar puncture is not routinely indicated as an immediate first step unless there are specific neurological signs or high suspicion of CNS infection.

questions.explanation: This child presents with febrile neutropenia, defined as fever (single oral temperature ≥38.3°C or a temperature ≥38.0°C sustained for >1 hour) and neutropenia (ANC <500 cells/µL or ANC expected to fall to <500 cells/µL within 48 hours). Febrile neutropenia is a medical emergency in oncology patients, and immediate administration of empirical intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics (typically antipseudomonal, e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime) after obtaining blood cultures is crucial to prevent rapid progression to sepsis and septic shock, even in the absence of localizing signs. Delay in antibiotic administration significantly increases mortality. Oral antibiotics are generally reserved for very low-risk cases after an initial period of observation or in specific outpatient management protocols, which is not the immediate step for a presenting febrile neutropenic child. Observation without antibiotics is dangerous. A full septic work-up including lumbar puncture is not routinely indicated as an immediate first step unless there are specific neurological signs or high suspicion of CNS infection.
questions.hint: Febrile neutropenia in oncology patients requires immediate IV antibiotics after blood cultures.

questions.question: A 5-year-old child presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe headache, vomiting, and altered sensorium. On examination, there is neck stiffness and petechial rash. Which of the following is the MOST likely causative organism responsible for this pediatric emergency?

options.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is a less common cause of meningitis in children and does not typically present with petechial rash.
Haemophilus influenzae type b was a common cause of meningitis in children before vaccination, but it rarely presents with petechial rash.
Neisseria meningitidis is the most likely causative organism for meningitis with petechial rash due to its association with meningococcemia.
Streptococcus pneumoniae can cause meningitis but is less likely to present with petechial rash compared to Neisseria meningitidis.

questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of sudden onset severe headache, vomiting, altered sensorium, neck stiffness, and petechial rash is classic for meningococcal meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitidis. This organism is known for its rapid progression and high mortality if untreated.
questions.hint: Consider organisms causing meningitis with petechial rash.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy undergoing chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia presents with a fever of 38.5°C and an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 450 cells/µL. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Administer antipyretics and observe at home.
options.explanation: Antipyretics alone are insufficient in neutropenic fever; observation without antibiotics is unsafe.
Oral antibiotics may not achieve adequate serum levels in neutropenic patients; IV antibiotics are preferred.

options.text: Obtain blood cultures and initiate empiric intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics.
options.explanation: This is the standard of care for neutropenic fever to cover gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.
G-CSF is not the initial step; it may be considered later if neutropenia persists or for severe infections.

questions.explanation: This patient has neutropenic fever, which is a medical emergency requiring immediate empiric intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics after obtaining blood cultures to cover potential bacterial infections.
questions.hint: Neutropenic fever in a child with chemotherapy requires urgent antibiotic therapy.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy with newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma develops rapid electrolyte abnormalities after initiation of chemotherapy. Which of the following is NOT a characteristic metabolic derangement seen in Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS)?

options.explanation: Hyperkalemia is a hallmark of TLS due to the release of intracellular potassium from lysed tumor cells.
Hyperphosphatemia occurs due to the release of intracellular phosphate from lysed tumor cells.
Hyperuricemia results from the breakdown of nucleic acids into uric acid during tumor cell lysis.
Hypoglycemia is not a primary metabolic derangement associated with TLS.

questions.explanation: Tumor Lysis Syndrome is characterized by the rapid breakdown of tumor cells, leading to the release of intracellular contents. This results in hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hyperuricemia. The increased phosphate can bind with calcium, leading to secondary hypocalcemia. Hypoglycemia is not a primary metabolic derangement associated with TLS, although it can occur in critically ill children for other reasons.
questions.hint: Consider the metabolic consequences of rapid tumor cell breakdown.

questions.question: A 5-year-old child undergoing chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia presents to the emergency department with a temperature of 38.5°C and an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 400 cells/µL. What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Administer oral antibiotics and discharge home with close follow-up.
options.explanation: Oral antibiotics are insufficient in febrile neutropenia due to the risk of rapid progression to sepsis.

options.text: Initiate intravenous fluids and observe in the emergency department for 6-8 hours.
options.explanation: Observation alone is inadequate; empiric antibiotics must be started immediately.

options.text: Obtain blood cultures and administer empiric broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics.
options.explanation: This is the standard of care for febrile neutropenia to cover potential bacterial pathogens.

options.text: Administer antipyretics and schedule an outpatient clinic appointment the next day.
options.explanation: Delaying treatment in febrile neutropenia can lead to life-threatening complications.

questions.explanation: Febrile neutropenia in an oncology patient is a medical emergency. The most appropriate initial management involves promptly obtaining blood cultures to identify potential pathogens, followed immediately by the administration of empiric broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics to cover common bacterial pathogens, as sepsis can rapidly progress. Delay in antibiotic administration significantly increases mortality risk.
questions.hint: Febrile neutropenia requires urgent intervention to prevent sepsis.

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy presents with facial swelling, distended neck veins, cough, and respiratory distress. On examination, he has a plethoric face and prominent collateral veins over the chest. His mother reports he has been increasingly irritable and sleepy. Which of the following is the most likely underlying oncologic emergency?

options.explanation: Hyperleukocytosis causes respiratory distress and CNS symptoms but not the specific venous obstruction signs seen here.
Spinal cord compression would present with neurological deficits in the limbs, not facial swelling or distended neck veins.
SVCS is characterized by facial swelling, distended neck veins, and collateral veins due to obstruction of the superior vena cava.
TLS is a metabolic emergency, not associated with facial swelling or venous obstruction.

questions.explanation: The constellation of facial swelling, distended neck veins, cough, respiratory distress, and prominent chest collateral veins in a child with a potential underlying malignancy is classic for Superior Vena Cava Syndrome (SVCS). The irritability and sleepiness suggest potential cerebral edema due to impaired venous drainage. Hyperleukocytosis would primarily cause respiratory distress and CNS symptoms but not the specific venous obstruction signs. Spinal cord compression would present with neurological deficits in the limbs. TLS is a metabolic emergency.
questions.hint: Consider the anatomical and clinical features of venous obstruction.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 6-month-old infant with newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia presents with a WBC count of 350,000 cells/µL, respiratory distress, and altered mental status. Funduscopic examination reveals retinal hemorrhages. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapeutic intervention to prevent further complications?

options.text: Immediate radiation therapy to the brain.
options.explanation: Radiation therapy is not the initial treatment for leukostasis; it is used for localized disease control.
Platelet transfusions are for bleeding due to thrombocytopenia, not for reducing leukostasis.
Exchange transfusion or leukapheresis rapidly reduces the circulating blast count and prevents complications like intracranial hemorrhage or respiratory failure.
Corticosteroids are not the primary treatment for symptomatic leukostasis, though they may be used as part of chemotherapy.

questions.explanation: This patient is presenting with symptomatic hyperleukocytosis (leukostasis), characterized by a very high WBC count leading to circulatory impairment in vital organs (lungs, brain). Exchange transfusion or leukapheresis is the most effective initial intervention to rapidly reduce the circulating blast count and prevent further life-threatening complications like intracranial hemorrhage or respiratory failure. Radiation therapy is not an acute intervention for leukostasis. Platelet transfusions are for bleeding due to thrombocytopenia, not primarily for leukostasis. Corticosteroids are not the primary treatment for symptomatic leukostasis, though they may be used as part of chemotherapy.
questions.hint: Leukostasis requires urgent reduction of circulating blasts to prevent organ damage.

questions.question: A 10-year-old girl with a history of Ewing sarcoma presents with acute onset back pain radiating to her legs, progressive leg weakness, and urinary retention. On examination, she has decreased sensation below T10. What is the most critical immediate management step?

options.explanation: MRI is the gold standard for diagnosing spinal cord compression and guiding urgent intervention.
While corticosteroids may be used, imaging is the immediate priority to confirm the diagnosis.
Surgery is indicated if compression is confirmed, but imaging must be done first.
Radiation therapy is a treatment option but not the immediate step; imaging is required first.

questions.explanation: The patient's symptoms suggest spinal cord compression, a medical emergency. Immediate imaging (MRI) is required to confirm the diagnosis and guide further management, including potential surgical decompression or radiotherapy. Delay in diagnosis can lead to permanent neurological deficits.
questions.hint: Spinal cord compression requires urgent imaging to prevent permanent damage.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy undergoing chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia presents to the emergency department with a fever of 38.5°C. His absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is 400 cells/µL. What is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Administer antipyretics and observe for 24 hours.
options.explanation: Observation without immediate antibiotics is inappropriate in febrile neutropenia due to high risk of severe infection.

options.text: Obtain blood cultures and start broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics immediately.
options.explanation: This is the correct initial step in managing febrile neutropenia to cover potential pathogens and prevent sepsis.

options.text: Obtain a chest X-ray and start oral antibiotics.
options.explanation: Oral antibiotics are insufficient, and chest X-ray is not the priority in this emergency.

options.text: Send for complete blood count and wait for results before initiating treatment.
options.explanation: Waiting for lab results delays critical antibiotic administration, increasing mortality risk.

questions.explanation: Febrile neutropenia (fever with ANC < 500 cells/µL or < 1000 cells/µL and predicted to fall) is a life-threatening emergency in oncology patients. The most appropriate initial management is to obtain blood cultures (from all lumens if a central line is present) and immediately initiate empiric, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics to cover common pathogens, typically Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Delaying antibiotic administration significantly increases morbidity and mortality.
questions.hint: Consider the urgency of antibiotic administration in febrile neutropenia.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 10-year-old girl with newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma is started on chemotherapy. 24 hours later, she develops lethargy, muscle cramps, and dark urine. Laboratory investigations reveal hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and hyperuricemia. Which of the following is the most critical immediate intervention in her management?

options.explanation: Phosphate binders are supportive but not the most critical immediate intervention.
This is the cornerstone of initial management for TLS to prevent renal failure and reduce uric acid levels.
Calcium gluconate is used for symptomatic hypocalcemia but is not the primary intervention for TLS.
Sodium bicarbonate may be used to alkalinize urine but is not the most critical immediate step.

questions.explanation: This patient is presenting with classic features and laboratory findings of Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS), a metabolic emergency caused by rapid lysis of malignant cells. The most critical immediate intervention is aggressive intravenous hydration to promote renal excretion of metabolites and prevent acute kidney injury, combined with allopurinol (or rasburicase in high-risk cases) to reduce uric acid production and prevent uric acid nephropathy.
questions.hint: Focus on the immediate metabolic derangements and their management in TLS.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy presents with facial puffiness, distended neck veins, and difficulty breathing, worsening over the past 2 days. He has a history of an anterior mediastinal mass diagnosed two weeks ago, pending biopsy. On examination, he has stridor and a positive Pemberton's sign. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic and therapeutic approach?

options.text: Immediately start corticosteroids and prepare for emergency intubation.
options.explanation: This is the correct initial approach to stabilize the patient and prevent respiratory arrest.

options.text: Proceed with urgent CT-guided biopsy of the mediastinal mass.
options.explanation: Biopsy should be deferred until the patient is stabilized due to the risk of precipitating cardiorespiratory arrest.

options.text: Administer diuretics and perform a diagnostic thoracentesis.
options.explanation: Diuretics are contraindicated in SVC syndrome as they can worsen fluid retention and airway compromise.

options.text: Obtain an urgent MRI and start empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics.
options.explanation: Antibiotics are not the priority in SVC syndrome, and MRI should not delay immediate stabilization.

questions.explanation: The patient's presentation is highly suggestive of Superior Vena Cava (SVC) syndrome, likely due to compression by the anterior mediastinal mass. This is a life-threatening emergency, particularly with airway compromise (stridor). The immediate priority is to stabilize the patient. High-dose corticosteroids should be administered promptly to reduce tumor bulk and inflammation, which can alleviate airway compression. Simultaneously, preparations for emergency airway management, including intubation, should be made given the stridor.
questions.hint: Consider the urgency of airway management and the role of corticosteroids in SVC syndrome.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy with a known history of neuroblastoma presents with acute onset back pain, progressive weakness in both lower limbs, and urinary incontinence over the past 12 hours. On examination, he has decreased tone and power (2/5) in both lower limbs, diminished deep tendon reflexes, and a sensory level at T10. What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.explanation: This is the correct immediate step to reduce spinal cord edema and prevent irreversible damage.

options.text: Schedule an urgent MRI of the entire spine.
options.explanation: While MRI is essential, corticosteroids should be administered immediately without delay.

options.text: Perform an emergent lumbar puncture to rule out leptomeningeal disease.
options.explanation: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in suspected cord compression until imaging rules out an obstructive lesion.

options.text: Prepare for surgical decompression within 24-48 hours.
options.explanation: Surgical decompression is a later step after stabilization and imaging; corticosteroids are the immediate priority.

questions.explanation: This patient presents with classic signs and symptoms of acute spinal cord compression (back pain, progressive motor weakness, sensory level, bladder dysfunction) in the context of an underlying malignancy (neuroblastoma). Spinal cord compression is a medical emergency requiring rapid intervention to prevent irreversible neurological damage. The most appropriate immediate next step is to administer high-dose intravenous corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone) to reduce peritumoral edema and inflammation, which can alleviate pressure on the spinal cord.
questions.hint: Consider the urgency of corticosteroids in acute spinal cord compression to prevent permanent damage.
questions.subject: neet-pg-pediatrics
